column6: The commentary treats the person himself as the final lost capital; Jesus asks what gain there is in winning the whole world while losing oneself.
The rich man counts years of stored goods as security, but his life is required that night; the scene makes the commentary's hidden loss of principal concrete.
This parallel rich-fool saying has a man plan to fill his stores and lack nothing, then die that night; it sharpens the gap between expected profit and the actual account.
Laodicea says it is rich and needs nothing yet does not know it is poor and wretched; this enacts the commentary's loss that can grow unseen beneath apparent success.
After a long interval the master returns and settles accounts with servants entrusted with capital; the parable joins time, work and final reckoning as in the commentary's market image.
The speakers plan to travel, trade and make a profit for a year; James places the commentary's merchant's forecast inside the uncertainty of human life.
James says people do not know tomorrow and their life is a brief vapor; this supplies the finite lifetime that the commentary calls the capital being spent.

column5: riches kept to their owner's hurt
column6: Qohelet says wealth can be kept to the owner's harm, directly matching the commentary's principal that diminishes even while a person appears to possess it.

column5: wealth lost in a bad venture
column6: A failed venture makes the rich man lose his property and leave nothing to his son; this gives the commentary's unprofitable trade a concrete household consequence.

column5: wealth amassed without knowing its heir
column6: The fleeting human heaps up riches without knowing who will gather them; this joins the commentary's passing lifetime to its image of capital that cannot be kept.

column5: wages in a bag with holes
column6: Haggai says people earn wages only to put them into a pierced bag; the image makes the commentary's principal loss visible in an apparently completed day's work.
The rich man says he can now enjoy his goods but does not know how soon he will die and leave them; this is a Jewish parallel to the commentary's false confidence in accumulated capital.
The speaker asks what wealth and pride profited the wicked, then says it passed like a shadow; the text explicitly judges apparent gain by what remains.

column5: labor spent on what cannot satisfy
column6: Isaiah asks why people spend money on what is not bread and labor for what does not satisfy; this directly tests the commentary's unprofitable trade and wasted life-capital.

column5: short day, much work, great reward
column6: Rabbi Tarfon's saying makes the day short, the work much and the reward great; it turns the commentary's time-as-capital image into an explicit account of finite time and labor.

column5: an hour of deeds and repentance
column6: The Mishnah values one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world above the whole life of the world to come; it makes each unit of time consequential as in the commentary's account.
The teaching to repent one day before death is answered by the uncertainty of that day, so one should repent today; it gives the commentary's passing time an urgent, practical consequence.
Paul says a person's work may burn and he will suffer loss; this gives the commentary's final accounting a specific test of what a lifetime's work actually yielded.
All things are exposed before God, to whom people must give account; this complements the commentary's contrast between visible success and an unseen loss.
Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory; the wording gives the commentary's comprehensive human deficit a specific moral and theological measure.
God repays each according to deeds; this connects the commentary's person-in-loss to its neighboring ayah's faith and action as the basis of the final account.
Paul says God shows no partiality; with the preceding verse's judgment by deeds, this matches the commentary's refusal to distinguish people by lineage or rank.

column5: no preference for rich or prince
column6: Elihu says God does not favor princes or the rich over the poor, since all are his handiwork; this closely matches the commentary's human class that cuts across social rank.
The merchants shrink the measure, enlarge the shekel and falsify the scales; this is the commentary's specific image of making another person's purchase come up short.

column5: buying the needy and selling sweepings
column6: The merchants exploit the poor and sell the grain's sweepings; this shows the human cost of the under-measure that the commentary describes as taking another's principal.
Proverbs calls a false balance abhorrent and a just weight pleasing to God, joining the commentary's market scale to moral judgment.
Israel is commanded to use just balances, weights and measures; this supplies the positive counterpart to the commentary's trader who secretly gives less than was paid for.

column5: Job asks to be weighed fairly
column6: Job asks to be weighed in just balances so God may know his integrity; the speaker's appeal makes the market scale an image for testing a person's standing.

column5: God weighs what people cannot see
column6: A person's ways seem pure in their own eyes, but the Lord weighs the spirit; this directly answers the commentary's unaware loser who thinks his account is sound.
The solitary worker has no heir, never stops laboring and deprives himself of good; this joins the commentary's isolated human, depleted capital and loss of self.
Qohelet says two are better than one because they have a good return for their toil; this counters the commentary's solitary person in loss with benefit made possible by companionship.
If one falls, the other can lift him; this gives concrete form to the commentary's claim that people leave isolation through mutual relation.

column5: speak truth as members of one another
column6: Paul commands each person to speak truth to a neighbor because they are members of one another; this closely meets the commentary's transition from an isolated human to reciprocal counsel in truth.
The community must exhort one another daily so none is hardened by sin; this links reciprocal counsel to the commentary's time-limited escape from loss.
Paul says what a person sows is what that person will reap; the harvest image makes the commentary's labor-and-account metaphor a concrete rule of consequence.
Sowing to the flesh yields corruption, while sowing to the Spirit yields eternal life; this distinguishes loss from lasting gain by the kind of life invested.
Paul urges persistence in doing good because the harvest comes in due time; this connects the commentary's finite time and good work to patient endurance.
Job calls human life on earth hard service and its days those of a hired worker; this is an unusually close image for the commentary's human spending time as capital and receiving a day's wage.

column5: short human life full of trouble
column6: Job says a human born of woman has few days and much trouble; this gives the commentary's universal human condition a concrete account of brief, burdened life.
Adam must eat from cursed ground through painful toil all the days of his life; this connects the commentary's account of human loss with labor that consumes a finite life.

column5: sweat, bread and return to dust
column6: The human eats bread by sweat until returning to the dust; this places work and death together as the commentary does when it calls time the principal spent.

column5: fixed days and an impassable limit
column6: Job says a person's days are determined and their boundary cannot be crossed; this makes explicit the due term that the commentary associates with each person's final account.
The house built by one who hears and does Jesus' words withstands rain, flood and wind; this brings together the commentary's shelter, storm and distinction by action.
The house of the one who hears but does not do collapses under rain, flood and wind; this is a concrete image of loss tied to the deed that the commentary says changes one's outcome.

Jesus concludes the rich fool story with the person who stores up for himself but is not rich toward God; this states the commentary's distinction between visible accumulation and a sound final account.
The vineyard owner gives the last workers the same denarius as the first; this revises a strict market ledger by making the kingdom's reward rest on the giver's generosity, not hours worked.

Paul contrasts visible things, which are temporary, with unseen things, which are eternal; this illuminates the commentary's tension between the visible human and a loss or value that sight alone misses.

column5: אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
column6: The commentary's source word is ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ; Job calls the wage-bound mortal אֱנוֹשׁ. The table notes BDB's Arabic cognate, while Job's hired-worker image adds the short, allotted human day.

column5: אנוש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
column6: The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity in loss; Psalm 8 calls the mortal אֱנוֹשׁ and asks why God remembers him, keeping the source's mortality term within a text of divine regard.

The commentary's ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ names humanity; Daniel's Aramaic humanlike figure appears with the clouds before the Ancient of Days among beastly kingdoms. The table's sound match is unverified; this is a distinct apocalyptic human image, not an identity.

column5: Daniel's humanlike figure applied to Jesus
column6: Jesus applies Daniel's cloud-coming human figure to himself before the council and speaks of vindication and authority; this Christian reading makes the humanlike figure's dominion a reply to defeat and loss.

The source commentary's Arabic خُسْرٍ names loss; Qohelet uses מְחַסֵּר for depriving one's own self of good amid fruitless solitary labor. This is a candidate root correspondence, not proof of cognacy.

The source word خُسْرٍ names loss; Daniel says the king was weighed and found חַסִּיר, deficient. The table's unverified Aramaic sound match is reinforced by the passage's exact image of judgment by measure.

The commentary's neighboring exception says وَعَمِلُوا۟, righteous action as labor in the profitable trade; Qohelet asks what gain a person gets from עָמָל beneath the sun, exposing toil without surplus.

The commentary links its neighboring بِٱلْحَقِّ to the day that brings each person to a term; Job uses חֻקָּיו for the fixed bounds of human days. The sound correspondence is unverified, but the allotted-limit motif is specific.

column5: אנש (table correspondence; BDB notes Arabic cognate)
column6: The commentary says the human named by ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ can fail to see his own loss; Jeremiah calls the heart אָנֻשׁ, desperately sick, and asks who can understand it, joining the table's weak/ill form to self-ignorance.

The source commentary's خُسْرٍ is an account of loss; Proverbs warns that one rushing after wealth will not know that חֶסֶר, want, will come. This joins hidden deficit to pursuit of gain without claiming cognacy.

The source commentary places the human in indefinite loss; Moses describes the promised land as one in which Israel will lack nothing. The table correspondence is unverified, and the verse offers a concrete counter-image of sufficiency.

The commentary's separate source image under عَصْر includes pressing and storm; Job says God can withhold waters until drought or release them until the land is overwhelmed. The table's עָצַר means restrain, a related but unverified sound correspondence.

column5: seeing another's eye, missing one's own
column6: Jesus pictures a person noticing a speck in a brother's eye while ignoring a beam in his own; this echoes the commentary's eye imagery and its warning that the person may not see his own condition.
The hearer who looks in a mirror goes away and forgets what he looks like; this gives a specific image for the commentary's claim that a person may fail to see himself without another's reflection.

column5: treasure vulnerable to decay and theft
column6: Jesus warns that earthly treasure is eaten by moth and rust or stolen; this gives physical form to the commentary's principal that can diminish while a person thinks he is accumulating.

The commentary's separate B008 image records a closed-mouthed vessel under عَصْر; Genesis says God had shut Abimelech's women's wombs, using עָצַר, restrain/close. This is only a shared closure image, not evidence that the Arabic word means loss by closure.
